records.sourceFile: Comparative Effectiveness of Exercise Interventions for Hamstring Injury Prevention in Football Players - A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Hong B, Hong X, Lin H, Yang Z, Feng J. Comparative Effectiveness of Exercise Interventions for Hamstring Injury Prevention in Football Players: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine - Open. 2026;12:135.
paper.abstract: Eleven randomized controlled trials (9,282 football players) were pooled in a random-effects network meta-analysis of exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programs. FIFA 11+ had the most consistent association with lower hamstring injury incidence than usual training (IRR 0.55, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.98), but certainty ranged from low to very low. Because no trials compared active interventions directly, the ranking rests on indirect comparisons through usual training.
paper.tldr: Across 11 football trials (9,282 players), FIFA 11+ was the only program whose 95% confidence interval stayed below 1 versus usual training (IRR 0.55). Certainty is low to very low, so it can be considered as a whole-team warm-up, not as a proven ranking over NHE.
paper.methods: PRISMA-aligned systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420251243576) of randomized controlled trials, searching PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase and Web of Science to January 5, 2026. Random-effects network meta-analysis of incidence rate ratios (IRR) versus usual training, with P-scores, RoB 2 risk of bias, GRADE/CINeMA certainty, and male-only, age-stratified and injury-definition sensitivity analyses.
paper.findings: FIFA 11+ had an IRR of 0.55 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.98) versus usual training and the highest P-score (0.84), while FIFA 11+ Kids (IRR 0.43, 95% CI 0.08 to 2.32) rests on a single trial. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial (I2 72.4%), and in the time-loss-only sensitivity analysis FIFA 11+ was no longer significant (IRR 0.65, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.12). In the male-only analysis FIFA 11+ stayed significant (IRR 0.56, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.91).
paper.limitations: Certainty was low to very low for the primary comparisons, and 3 of 11 trials were at high risk of bias with none at low risk. The network is star-shaped with no direct active comparisons, and several nodes rest on one trial. Table 1 lists identical exposure hours (66,423 and 65,725) for two different trials (Steffen 2008 and van de Hoef 2019), which may be a transcription error the authors should check.
paper.practicalImplications: FIFA 11+ may be considered a scalable whole-team warm-up because it showed the most consistent signal in this network, but the authors stress that its value is its standardized team format rather than proven superiority. The authors also suggest that targeted progressive eccentric work, including NHE, may be prioritized for players with prior injury or low eccentric knee-flexor strength, though this was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: The paper supports FIFA 11+ as a practical team-wide warm-up, but it does not show that FIFA 11+ beats NHE because no trial compared them directly. Using NHE as a targeted add-on for high-risk players is a hypothesis the trials did not test.
paper.rtp: It cannot inform return to sport. Every included trial measured hamstring injury incidence for prevention in players, with no rehabilitation, readiness or re-injury outcomes, so it cannot set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Mechanisms, injury patterns, and kinematic features of hamstring strain injuries in football (soccer) - a systematic review and meta-analysis of video-analysis studies.pdf

paper.citation: Xia J, He J, Yao J, Zhu Y, Mao L, Zhu X. Mechanisms, injury patterns, and kinematic features of hamstring strain injuries in football (soccer): a systematic review and meta-analysis of video-analysis studies. Front Public Health. 2026;14:1846524.
paper.abstract: This meta-analysis pooled seven football match video-analysis studies of 342 hamstring strain injuries. Non-contact and sprint-type injuries were reported more often than indirect-contact and mixed-type injuries. Offensive vs defensive phase, first vs second half, and sprint vs stretch mechanisms showed no clear difference.
paper.tldr: Match video studies of football hamstring injuries most often describe non-contact, sprint-type events. The evidence is small and inconsistent, and it cannot show which training or prevention strategies would reduce these injuries.
paper.methods: Seven databases were searched to 12 February 2026, and the protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261335634) after the preliminary search but before screening. Eligible studies used video analysis of real-match hamstring injuries in 11-a-side football, and five prespecified odds ratios were pooled with DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models restricted to male samples. Single-arm proportions were pooled with a generalized linear mixed model, and quality was rated with JBI, STROBE-SIIS and QA-SIVAS.
paper.findings: Non-contact vs indirect contact gave OR 2.51 (95% CI 1.31 to 4.82, p = 0.006, I2 = 71%), and sprint-type vs mixed-type gave OR 2.01 (95% CI 1.04 to 3.87, p = 0.037, I2 = 67%). Sprint vs stretch (OR 1.64, 95% CI 0.74 to 3.61), offensive vs defensive (OR 0.99) and first vs second half (OR 1.13) showed no clear difference. Kinematic and sex comparisons were exploratory, and no sex difference survived multiple-comparison correction.
paper.limitations: Only seven studies and 342 cases were included, with mechanism definitions and video standards that differ across studies. Four of the seven were rated high risk of bias by JBI, and the two significant results rest on nominal p values with wide confidence intervals. The female evidence comes from one study, so sex comparisons are descriptive only.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use the pattern of non-contact, sprint-type events to frame questions about high-speed running exposure, eccentric load tolerance and single-leg support in monitoring and prevention work. The paper does not show that any specific exercise, dose or load reduces hamstring injury.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the pattern points to high-speed running and late-swing eccentric loading as the setting to examine when reviewing sprint exposure and eccentric tolerance. The review gives no dose, load or exercise prescription and reports no training effect on hamstring injury.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes how hamstring injuries happen in match play and reports no recovery, readiness, re-injury or return-timing data, so use it only as background on injury mechanism.

records.sourceFile: Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Gu J, Li Y, Wang Y, Zhang Y. Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Ann Med. 2026;58(1):2652116.
paper.abstract: This meta-analysis pooled 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) of exercise-based hamstring injury prevention in football. Programmes reduced hamstring strain risk, and the effect was largest in trials where at least 75% of prescribed sessions were completed. Programme type and components could not be reliably separated.
paper.tldr: Exercise-based hamstring prevention roughly halved hamstring strain risk across 15 football trials, but a clear benefit appeared only in trials where most prescribed sessions were completed. The review cannot say which programme type or component works best.
paper.methods: Six databases were searched to 1 October 2025 (PROSPERO CRD420251246295) for randomised and cluster-randomised trials comparing an exercise-based hamstring prevention programme with usual practice or a standard warm-up in football participants. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled risk ratios, with prespecified subgroup analyses and meta-regression for training dose, adherence and playing level, and quality was judged with RoB 2 and GRADE.
paper.findings: The overall RR was 0.51 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.71), equal to 38 fewer hamstring injuries per 1000 participants on a control event rate of 7.8% (95% CI 23 to 50 fewer). High adherence (at least 75%) gave RR 0.36 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.48), against RR 0.92 (95% CI 0.68 to 1.23) for low adherence (P for interaction below 0.00001). Meta-regression across 14 trials gave an RR multiplier of 0.83 per 10 percentage points of adherence, while training frequency and weekly volume did not change the effect.
paper.limitations: Heterogeneity was moderate (I2 57%) with a prediction interval crossing the null, and the subgroup and meta-regression results are study-level and exploratory. The Discussion states that residual heterogeneity falls close to zero after adding adherence, but no residual I2 or tau2 is reported in the Results, so that claim cannot be checked. Trim-and-fill gave an adjusted RR of 0.54 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.75), and the certainty of evidence was rated low.
paper.practicalImplications: Monitor programme session completion, because a clear benefit was seen only in trials with high adherence (at least 75% of prescribed sessions). Within the 1 to 4 sessions per week and 1 to 60 minutes per week range studied, higher frequency or volume gave no clear extra benefit, so lower-frequency plans can work if they are delivered consistently. The review does not show that one programme type or exercise component is superior to another.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the practical point is that protection was associated with high programme completion at the trial level, so completion should be tracked alongside the prescription. Trials prescribing 1 to 2 sessions per week were about as protective as those prescribing 3 to 4 (RR 0.56 vs 0.45). The review cannot choose between Nordic hamstring, FIFA 11+ or other programme types, and dose metrics differ across trials.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It studies prevention in football participants, not injured players, excludes rehabilitation and post-surgical interventions, and reports no return-to-play timing, readiness or post-injury outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Situations Leading to Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury in Sports - A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Mai P, Willwacher S, Rahlf L, Hoenig T, Braun L, von Diecken C, et al. Situations Leading to Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury in Sports: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2026;56:2139-2160.
paper.abstract: Thirty-nine video-analysis studies (1551 video-verified ACL injuries) were pooled across sports. Noncontact (n = 745), indirect contact (n = 533) and direct contact (n = 273) mechanisms were reported, and most injuries involved ball action, pressing/tackling or cutting, often during ball possession and at high horizontal speed.
paper.tldr: Most ACL injuries in these team sports occurred without direct contact, most often while cutting, decelerating or landing, or while pressing or being tackled, and many happened with the ball in possession. Use this to choose which situations to rehearse in each sport, not as a measure of how risky those situations are.
paper.methods: Systematic review with meta-analysis (PRISMA; PROSPERO CRD42022337340) of video-analysis studies of ACL injuries in athletes of any sex during training or competition, searched in PubMed, Google Scholar (first 200 entries), Web of Science and Scopus, with searches run in April 2023 and updated in August 2025. Random-effects pooled proportions were calculated for movement pattern, movement speed and game situation, with sport tested as a moderator where at least three studies were available, and study quality was rated with QA-SIVAS.
paper.findings: Of 1551 injuries, 44.0% were pooled as noncontact, 36.4% as indirect contact and 19.5% as direct contact. Among noncontact injuries, cutting (53.8%), pressing/tackling (50.2%), deceleration (38.9%) and landing (30.1%) were most common, and 70.7% occurred at high horizontal speed. Indirect contact injuries most often involved being tackled (56.1%), and among the team sports direct contact was most common in contact-oriented football (32.1%) compared with soccer (22.5%) and basketball (6.1%), with the single judo study higher still (64.7%).
paper.limitations: The results are proportions of injuries, not incidence or risk, because the review has no exposure denominators, and overlapping categories mean percentages do not sum to 100. Quality varied (QA-SIVAS 33-83%, with 10 of 39 studies below 60%), most injuries were in men (79.2%), most samples were highly trained, and the early-match clustering in football (37.5%, two studies) and netball (37.8%, one study) rests on very few studies.
paper.practicalImplications: For sports with mostly noncontact injuries, the authors' recommendations are cutting, braking and single- and double-leg landing technique at match speed, eccentric strength, and drills with the ball and decision-making demands. For contact sports, the pooled data point to tackle-related exposures in contact-oriented football and to perturbation drills for indirect contact injuries, but the review does not test whether these reduce injury.
paper.athleteDev: Supports sport-specific prevention planning: cutting, deceleration and landing technique at high speed, eccentric strength, and game-speed drills with ball and decision-making demands. It gives no training-load, exposure or intervention data, so it cannot show which drill changes injury rates.
paper.rtp: It cannot inform return-to-sport timing, testing or clearance, because it reports the situations in which ACL injuries occurred and no return or re-injury outcomes. Rehabilitation staff may use the high-risk situations (cutting, landing, tackled contact) to choose what to rehearse before return, but the review does not show that such drills make return safer.

records.sourceFile: Lateral Extra-articular Procedures Reduce the Risk of Revision of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Elite Athletes - A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Comparative Studies.pdf

paper.citation: D'Ambrosi R, Carrozzo A, Monaco E, Sconfienza LM, Herbst E, Herbort M, et al. Lateral Extra-articular Procedures Reduce the Risk of Revision of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Elite Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Comparative Studies. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026;54(2):457-464.
paper.abstract: Four comparative studies of elite athletes (586 with isolated ACL reconstruction, 417 with ACL reconstruction plus a lateral extra-articular procedure) were pooled. Ipsilateral rerupture was 14.0% with isolated reconstruction and 5.0% with the added procedure, and the pooled odds ratio was 0.35 (95% CI 0.20-0.59).
paper.tldr: In four small comparative studies of elite athletes, adding a lateral extra-articular procedure to ACL reconstruction was linked to fewer reruptures (5.0% vs 14.0%). Treat this as a reason to discuss the option with the surgeon, not as proof it works for every athlete.
paper.methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA, registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025637843), searching PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Library for comparative studies of rerupture in elite athletes after isolated ACL reconstruction versus reconstruction plus LEAP. Study quality was rated with MINORS (mean 15 +/- 0.8 points), and rerupture rates and odds ratios were pooled with random-effects models.
paper.findings: Rerupture was 14.0% with isolated reconstruction and 5.0% with reconstruction plus LEAP, a significant between-group difference (P = .042). The pooled odds ratio was 0.35 (95% CI 0.20-0.59; P < .001), which the authors describe as a 65% lower risk of rerupture, and funnel plot tests showed no asymmetry. Three included studies reported no difference in subsequent surgery between groups, and rehabilitation did not differ.
paper.limitations: Only four studies were included, all non-randomized comparative designs at level 3, and the authors cite the limited number of studies as a constraint. Graft choice, LEAP technique, attachment points and concomitant surgery varied, and mean follow-up was 2 to 3.7 years in three studies and 100 months in one. The conclusion's 'by .60%' is an extraction artifact for '>60%' (the text renders > as a period throughout); the reported result is an odds ratio of 0.35.
paper.practicalImplications: For an elite athlete facing ACL reconstruction, the surgical team can weigh adding a lateral extra-articular procedure as an option to discuss, because these four non-randomized studies reported fewer reruptures with it. The benefit is a rerupture difference only, so it should be weighed against the individual athlete's injury and the surgeon's judgement rather than applied as a routine step.
paper.athleteDev: Limited direct use for performance staff: the paper concerns the surgical decision made before rehabilitation, and it reports no training, load or performance outcomes. It is relevant only when a performance or medical team is asked whether an elite athlete's reconstructed ACL should be protected with an extra-articular procedure.
paper.rtp: It cannot inform return-to-sport timing, readiness or clearance, because return-to-sport outcomes are not reported in the results. Its only relevance is the surgical question of graft rerupture risk, which staff may weigh with the surgeon but which does not change return criteria.

records.sourceFile: Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for concussion - a systematic review and meta-analysis for the Female, woman and girl_or Athlete Injury pRevention (FAIR) consensus.pdf

paper.citation: Shill IJ, Shepherd HA, Eliason PH, Kolstad AT, Heyward O, Martens G, et al. Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for concussion: a systematic review and meta-analysis for the Female, woman and girl/or Athlete Injury pRevention (FAIR) consensus. Br J Sports Med. 2025:1599-1616.
paper.abstract: Systematic review with meta-analyses and GRADE of 108 studies on prevention strategies (67) and modifiable risk factors (41) for sport-related concussion and head impact events in female, woman and girl athletes. Evidence was mostly limited or very low certainty, and only 37% of studies gave female-specific estimates.
paper.tldr: Evidence for concussion prevention strategies and risk factors specific to female, woman and girl athletes is thin. The only protective signal is very low certainty support for headgear in adolescent lacrosse and soccer, while eyewear and artificial turf showed no concussion effect.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review with meta-analyses (PROSPERO CRD42023485808) searching eight databases (Medline, CINAHL, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, EMBASE, ERIC, CENTRAL and CDSR) from 2001 to October and November 2023. Eligible studies had original data, a comparison group, a prevention strategy or modifiable risk factor, and at least one female participant per group; quality was rated with the Downs and Black tool and certainty with GRADE. Random-effects meta-analyses were run when at least three studies gave female-specific estimates for similar exposures and outcomes (headgear, eyewear, field type).
paper.findings: Headgear was associated with lower concussion rates (intent-to-treat IRR 0.70, 95% CI 0.50-0.99; as-treated IRR 0.61, 95% CI 0.44-0.85), eyewear was not (IRR 1.08, 95% CI 0.69-1.68; I2 = 79%), and turf vs grass showed no difference (IRR 0.95, 95% CI 0.62-1.45), all very low certainty. Training studies with female-specific data were all in soccer and gave conflicting results for neck strengthening, and a youth soccer heading ban was followed by a higher proportion of concussion among injuries (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.01-1.69). Schools with athletic trainers reported higher concussion rates, which the authors suggest may reflect higher detection.
paper.limitations: Only 37% of studies gave female-specific estimates, no studies reported female Para athletes, and none of the female-specific prevention studies examined unintended consequences. Outcome definitions, interventions and exposure measures were heterogeneous, so most results could not be pooled. The planned NIH quality tools were replaced by the Downs and Black tool, a protocol deviation the authors report.
paper.practicalImplications: Headgear may be considered for adolescent female lacrosse and soccer players, but only as a very low certainty option. Protective eyewear cannot be recommended for concussion prevention, although it was linked to fewer eye, head and face injuries, and most other strategies need female-specific data before recommendations are made.
paper.athleteDev: The review gives no basis for changing training, playing surfaces or equipment to reduce concussion in female athletes beyond the very low certainty headgear signal. Neck strength findings were inconsistent and do not support neck training as a proven concussion prevention tool in women.
paper.rtp: Mainly concussion prevention evidence. Four management studies looked at time to return to play, but only with aggregated male and female data, so the review cannot guide return-to-play decisions for female athletes.

records.sourceFile: Comparative efficacy of portable active cooling vs. passive cooling for reducing core temperature in exertional heat stroke - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Shi C, Zhang T, Xia L, Shi W, Qu J, Song L, et al. Comparative efficacy of portable active cooling vs. passive cooling for reducing core temperature in exertional heat stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Public Health. 2026;14:1811173.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomized and crossover trials (148 participants) comparing portable active cooling with passive cooling for reducing core temperature in healthy volunteers with exercise-induced hyperthermia. External refrigerant-based devices cooled faster than passive cooling, while wearable pre-cooling vests did not.
paper.tldr: In healthy volunteers overheated by exercise, ice-water and other external refrigerant-based portable cooling lowered core temperature faster than resting in the shade, while cooling vests did not. None of the trials studied actual heat stroke, so this is about choosing a field device when cold-water immersion is not available, not about replacing it.
paper.methods: PRISMA 2020 review (PROSPERO CRD420261292698) searching PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Embase and MEDLINE to 20 January 2026 for randomized parallel or crossover trials in people aged 12 or older with exercise- or heat-induced core temperature elevation, comparing portable active cooling (type A: external refrigerant-based; type B: wearable pre-cooled) with passive cooling. The primary outcome was core cooling rate (C/min), pooled with random effects (generic inverse variance in RevMan 5.4, r = 0.5 assumed for crossover data), with subgroups by device type and ambient temperature and RoB 2 for crossover trials.
paper.findings: Active cooling cooled faster than passive cooling overall (MD 0.02 C/min, 95% CI 0.01-0.03, I2 88%). Type A devices were superior (MD 0.04 C/min, 95% CI 0.02-0.07), driven by ice-water tarp cooling (pooled difference 0.11 C/min, 2 studies; the paper words it as a 'cooling rate') rather than ice sheets or circulating blankets (MD 0.02 each), while type B vests showed no advantage (MD 0.00 C/min, 95% CI 0.00-0.01). The advantage appeared above 30 C ambient (MD 0.04) but not at 30 C or below (MD 0.01, p = 0.08), and three type A studies took about 5.9-9.3 min to lower core temperature by 1 C versus 25-26.6 min with passive cooling.
paper.limitations: Trials were small (10 to 18 participants) in healthy young adults with core temperature mostly below 40 C and no central nervous system dysfunction, so generalization to exertional heat stroke requires caution. All trials were high risk for lack of blinding, five were high risk for sequence generation, allocation concealment and outcome-assessor blinding were unreported, Egger's test suggested publication bias (p = 0.005), and safety reporting was incomplete. The abstract gives the type A confidence interval as 0.02-0.04, while the results report 0.02-0.07.
paper.practicalImplications: When cold-water immersion is not available in the field, an ice-water-soaked tarp or similar external refrigerant method cooled overheated volunteers much faster than passive rest, while pre-cooled vests added little. These are volunteer data, so heat stroke response plans should still keep cold-water immersion as the first-line treatment and watch for shivering, reported in up to 50% of participants in one ice-water study.
paper.athleteDev: For hot-weather training, the data suggest a wearable cooling vest does little beyond moving to a cool area and resting, while ice-water tarp cooling lowered core temperature faster in volunteers. Benefits were seen mainly when the ambient temperature was above 30 C.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-activity or clearance decisions after heat stroke, and cannot show treatment outcomes in clinical exertional heat stroke, because participants were healthy volunteers with exercise-induced hyperthermia and only cooling rate was measured.

records.sourceFile: 2025 Update to the Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement Part 2 - Clinical Guidelines for Screening, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Return to Play for Adolescents and Adults.pdf

paper.citation: Williams NI, De Souza MJ, Misra M, Nattiv A, Joy E, Barrack M, et al. 2025 Update to the Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement Part 2: Clinical Guidelines for Screening, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Return to Play for Adolescents and Adults. Sports Medicine. 2026;56:375-427.
paper.abstract: Second part of the 2025 Female Athlete Triad Coalition update, giving revised clinical guidelines for screening, diagnosis, treatment, and clearance and return to play for adolescent and adult female athletes. It covers eating disorders and disordered eating, non-pharmacological and pharmacological treatment of bone loss and menstrual disturbance, the addition of bone stress injury to the bone health spectrum, and an updated cumulative risk assessment with a new adolescent version.
paper.tldr: The 2025 Triad guidance asks staff to judge energy deficiency from serial weight, BMI, eating behaviour and, where possible, metabolic markers rather than an energy-availability threshold. A revised cumulative risk score guides physician clearance (0-1 points full clearance, 2-5 provisional or limited, 6 or more restricted), but the 2025 changes to the tool are not yet validated.
paper.methods: An independent expert panel of 16 clinicians, dietitians and scientists used a process similar to the 2014 consensus: one in-person meeting, several video meetings and e-mail, with section leaders drafting evidence-based statements from literature reviews. Statements were accepted by confidential online vote when more than 85% of writers agreed and none disagreed, and each was graded Level A (consistent RCT and/or observational data) to Level D (panel judgment).
paper.findings: Energy deficiency is now judged from serial changes in weight, BMI, EA, eating attitudes and, if resources allow, RMR ratio and hormones such as TT3; an EA threshold such as 30 kcal/kg FFM/day is not recommended, and an extra 300 to 600 kcal/day will likely initiate menstrual recovery (Level B), although resumed menses alone do not mean ovulation or normal ovarian hormones have returned. For bone, 12 months of refeeding (about 350 kcal/day) did not improve BMD in the REFUEL trial, transdermal estradiol with cyclic progestin improved BMD while combined oral contraceptives did not, and the panel recommends against combined oral contraceptives to improve bone or restore menses (Level A). The CRA scores six risk factors from 0 to 2, totals of 0-1, 2-5 and 6 or more map to full clearance, provisional or limited clearance, and restriction or disqualification, and the CRA score is graded as predictive of bone stress injury (Level B).
paper.limitations: Many statements rest on Level B or C evidence, and data on osteoanabolic, anti-resorptive and androgen therapies come mostly from anorexia nervosa samples, with studies in athletes lacking. The authors say the revised CRA scoring, substitutions and adolescent tool require further validation. The DXA recommendation is graded Level B in the text (Section 5.2.2) but Level A in the summary Table 12.
paper.practicalImplications: All female athletes should be screened for Triad risk factors, for example through the preparticipation physical evaluation, and a suspected eating disorder should be evaluated by a physician, a registered (ideally sports) dietitian and a mental health professional; the LEAF-Q should not be used on its own. Clearance decisions from the CRA should be made only by physicians, using written medical expectations agreements for high-risk athletes. For adolescents recovering from an eating disorder, return to play should start with socially oriented activity and practice, with competition allowed only once agreed weight status is reached and maintained.
paper.athleteDev: Performance and nutrition staff should track energy deficiency with serial body weight, BMI, eating behaviour and, where available, RMR ratio and TT3, rather than a single energy-availability cutoff, because weight can stay stable during energy deficiency. Athletes in lean sports (endurance, aesthetic, weight class) and those training 12 hours or more per week are flagged as higher-risk groups for regular screening.
paper.rtp: Directly relevant: the revised CRA and Figure 6 bands guide physician clearance for adult and adolescent female athletes, and the panel advises that athletes with anorexia nervosa and BMI below 16 kg/m2, or bulimia nervosa with purging more than four times a week, be categorically restricted from training and competition. For bone stress injury, higher MRI grade, trabecular-rich sites and high-risk sites (such as femoral neck, tarsal navicular, anterior tibial shaft and fifth metatarsal) are linked to delayed return to play and should be weighed alongside the CRA. Return-to-play guidance for eating pathology is a template based on limited evidence and should be individualised by the treatment team.
